newsitem.title: USA: Volunteers help take devil out of Devil's Night.
newsitem.headline: Volunteers help take devil out of Devil's Night.

text.p: Thousands of volunteers and a three-day gang truce helped city leaders take the spark out of "Devil's Night" arson for the second successive year Wednesday night, but high winds posed trouble for fighting the fires that were started.

City officials refused to disclose how many fires had been set Wednesday night, saying they wanted to make sure their count was accurate. But they indicated the count was down from last year, when 61 fires were set Oct. 30.

City spokesman Al Acker said many of the emergency workers on duty for Devil's Night were kept busy tending to downed power lines, trees and traffic light disruptions brought on by windy conditions that buffetted Michigan all day and into the evening.
"I would say that there's more activity along those lines than relative to any fire activity," he said.
About 30,000 volunteers wearing special orange hats patroled city streets in cars with yellow lights and CB radios to put an end to the annual ritual of setting fires the night before Halloween.
Mayor Dennis Archer spent the evening traversing the city, visiting neighbourhood centres and rallying citizen volunteers, who he said turned out in higher numbers than last year.
"There are a large number of volunteers all over the city. It doesn't matter what part you go to, you've got yellow lights," he said.
On Tuesday Rev. Robert Duggan, pastor of St. Anne Catholic Church, Detroit's oldest church, and an anti-gang activist brokererd a temporary truce between six gangs.

Still some firefighters spent the night battling blazes set in abandoned houses, sometimes by gang members. City workers demolished 850 abandoned houses in the weeks leading up to Devil's Night. Neighbours watching one house burn told WKBD-TV they had told the city repeatedly about the abandoned home, but to no avail.

Stamping out Devil's Night has become a priority of the Archer administration following a flareup in 1994, his first year in office. Archer failed to take the pre-emptive steps that his predecessor, Coleman Young, had done in the past, and the number of fires Oct. 30 jumped to 182 -- the highest in eight years.

Meanwhile the winds, some gusting as high as 50 mhp, knocked down about 400 power lines and cut off power to about 28,000 people in metro Detroit, utility officials said. Some 144,000 people across the state were left without power Wednesday night.
